claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by thermally induced surface segregation.
Heating toward the melting regime causes lower-melting-point elements such as copper to migrate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface migration creates a chemically inhomogeneous outer layer surrounding a more uniformly mixed core.
The segregated outer layer melts at a lower temperature than the uniformly mixed core.
The initially solid nanoparticles are homogeneous Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu solid solutions.
Slow sub-melting annealing permits selective elemental migration and promotes surface segregation.
Rapid post-synthesis quenching preserves compositional homogeneity by suppressing segregation.
The structural mediator is a copper-rich or otherwise lower-melting-element-rich surface layer whose composition differs from the particle interior.
Reduction of surface energy drives lower-melting-point elements to segregate preferentially to the nanoparticle surface during heating.
The segregated surface layer has weaker atomic bonding than the homogeneous material.
Weaker bonding in the segregated surface layer initiates premelting at a lower temperature than in the homogeneous core.
Pre-annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will exhibit a more extended premelting regime than rapidly quenched homogeneous controls.
Pre-annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will have a lower melting-onset temperature than rapidly quenched homogeneous controls.
Surface-energy and segregation effects dominate the thermal response in particles typically smaller than about 100 nm.
The proposed mechanism applies when the thermal history permits segregation without subsequent full homogenization during cooling.
